title: How to Measure Hiring Effectiveness: KPIs, Metrics & Best Practices
summary: Track quality of hire, time-to-fill, cost per hire, and candidate experience to transform recruiting from guesswork into data-driven operations.
body_text: When quarterly reports hit your desk, explaining hiring results without data hurts. You're defending empty seats while engineering projects stall and revenue targets slip. Nearly 70% of organizations face challenges recruiting for full-time positions, yet most can't quantify why their processes underperform. The problem isn't your recruiting team or the talent market; it's measurement. Without systematic KPI tracking, you're flying blind. You can't diagnose bottlenecks, justify budget requests, or prove ROI to leadership. Manual processes create delays you can't quantify, and candidate experience issues go undetected until Glassdoor reviews appear. Here's what you'll learn in this article: The Foundation: The five core dimensions of hiring effectiveness that reveal process bottlenecks Benchmark Your Performance: Seven essential KPIs with industry benchmarks and calculation formulas Pipeline Leak Detection: Supporting metrics that pinpoint exactly where qualified candidates drop off Implementation Roadmap: Best practices for implementing measurement systems that drive strategic action What Hiring Effectiveness Means To measure hiring effectiveness, track both efficiency and quality metrics. Efficiency metrics show speed and cost, while quality metrics reveal long-term hiring success and candidate experience. Efficiency Metrics Time-to-fill : Days from job opening to offer acceptance Cost per hire : Total recruiting investment divided by number of hires Offer acceptance rate : Percentage of candidates who accept your offers Quality Metrics Quality of hire : New employee performance, retention, and productivity Hiring manager satisfaction : Internal customer feedback on recruits and process Candidate Net Promoter Score : The Likelihood that candidates would recommend your company Source effectiveness: Which recruiting channels deliver the best hires These seven KPIs provide a complete view of recruiting performance from initial sourcing through retention. Each metric addresses specific bottlenecks in your hiring process. Why Activity Metrics Fail Enterprise Recruiting Counting interviews, phone screens, or LinkedIn messages feels productive but rarely predicts whether you'll land high-performing employees. Activity metrics create three critical blind spots: They reward busyness over outcomes. A recruiter scheduling 20 interviews per week looks productive, but if only one results in an offer, you're wasting hiring manager time and burning budget on volume instead of quality. They hide process breakdowns. High interview counts mask deeper problems: misaligned job requirements, poor candidate screening, or scheduling bottlenecks that let top talent accept competing offers. They can't justify the investment. Executives don't care how many resumes you reviewed. They want to know: Did we fill the role? Was it the right person? How much did it cost? SHRM's Hiring Difficulty Index dropped from 7.3 in Q4 2024 to 0.2 in Q2 2025, signaling improved market conditions. Yet organizations without measurement systems still can't diagnose why they miss hiring targets. When you shift measurement to offer acceptance rate, first-year retention, or hiring manager satisfaction, true process gaps become apparent, and you get a roadmap for operational fixes. Measuring Hiring Effectiveness: 5 Core Dimensions Successful recruiting teams track five interconnected dimensions that reveal how well your process converts open headcount into productive employees. 1. Speed Metrics show how quickly candidates move from application to offer. When time-to-hire drifts above market norms, top talent slips away . Benchmarks: 28-44 days (median) for most roles, 60-90 days for executive and specialized positions. 2. Quality Metrics combine performance ratings, hiring manager satisfaction, and retention to quantify fit. Track these against sourcing data to identify what produces high performers. 3. Cost Metrics translate recruiting activity into dollars. SHRM benchmarking data shows an average cost per hire of $4,700 , though total costs, including training, onboarding, and productivity loss, can reach 3-4x the position's salary for specialized and executive roles. Attribute every expense to see where to trim waste without cutting assessment rigor." 4. Experience Metrics capture how candidates feel about your process. A Candidate Net Promoter Score (cNPS) above +30 indicates positive experience. Monitor cNPS to repair communication gaps before they erode your employer brand. 5. Source Effectiveness Metrics show which channels deliver the best hires at optimal speed and cost. Seven Essential KPIs for Measuring Hiring Effectiveness Track these seven outcome-focused metrics to transform recruiting from guesswork into data-driven operations that deliver measurable ROI. 1. Time-to-Fill: Measuring Speed Without Sacrificing Quality Time-to-fill tracks calendar days from the requisition opening to the candidate's acceptance of the offer. This metric reveals scheduling bottlenecks, approval delays, and process inefficiencies that let top talent slip away to competitors. Industry Benchmarks: Entry-level and mid-level roles: 28-44 days (median) Specialized or senior roles: 44-60 days Executive roles: 60-90 days (median 60) Interview scheduling creates significant delays in traditional processes. When coordinating across multiple hiring managers and time zones, scheduling alone can consume two weeks. Organizations leveraging autonomous interview technologies report substantial time reductions, with some interviews occurring outside working hours. This 24/7 availability accelerates pipelines without increasing recruiter workload. Track time-to-fill by role type and department to identify specific bottlenecks. If engineering roles consistently exceed 60 days while sales roles fill in 30, investigate technical screening capacity and hiring manager availability. 2. Cost Per Hire: Understanding True Recruiting Expenses Cost per hire quantifies the total recruiting investment divided by the number of hires. This metric exposes hidden expenses and justifies technology investments through measurable ROI. Formula: (Internal Costs + External Costs) ÷ Number of Hires Cost Components: Internal: Recruiter salaries, hiring manager time, ATS subscriptions, employee referral bonuses External: Job board fees, agency commissions, background checks, recruiting events Industry Benchmarks: Standard roles: $1,200-$4,700 (median $1,244) Technical roles: $7,000-$12,000 Executive positions: $8,750-$35,000 (median $8,750) Focus on reducing efforts on process efficiency rather than assessment quality. Manual screening typically consumes 40-60% of recruiter time at typical hourly rates. Automated screening workflows eliminate these costs while maintaining evaluation rigor. Track cost per hire alongside quality of hire to ensure efficiency improvements don't compromise candidate quality. 3. Quality of Hire: Measuring Long-Term Success Quality of hire connects recruiting decisions to business performance through retention rates, performance ratings, and productivity metrics. This metric assesses whether your process identifies candidates who succeed in the long term. Formula: (Performance Rating + Hiring Manager Satisfaction + Retention Score) ÷ 3 Organizations typically establish internal benchmarks based on their performance rating systems, with scores above 80% considered high-quality and scores between 65% and 80% acceptable. Improve this metric by minimizing hiring bias via structured interviews and skills-based assessments. One talent acquisition director shared: "The AI interview felt natural and conversational. It asked follow-up questions based on my answers, just like talking to a real person." This type of consistent, unbiased evaluation improves quality scores across all roles. 4. Hiring Manager Satisfaction: Measuring Internal Customer Success Hiring manager satisfaction gauges whether recruiting delivers candidates who meet role requirements and process expectations. This metric reveals alignment issues between recruiters and hiring teams before they impact results. Measurement Method: Survey hiring managers within 90 days post-hire using 1-10 scale: Candidate quality and job fit Time-to-fill expectations Communication throughout the process Overall recruiting partnership Benchmark Ranges: Excellent: 8-10 (strong partnership) Acceptable: 6-7.5 (room for improvement) Critical: Below 6 (process breakdown) Low scores typically trace to unclear requirements, poor candidate quality, or communication gaps. Implement structured intake meetings to document role needs, technical requirements, team dynamics, and success criteria. When autonomous AI handles initial screening, recruiters gain bandwidth for strategic partnership and candidate experience. 5. Candidate Net Promoter Score: Protecting Employer Brand Candidate experience maintains employer brand and ensures high offer acceptance rates. Net Promoter Score measures whether candidates would recommend your organization based on their recruiting experience. Measurement Method: Ask all candidates post-decision: "How likely would you recommend [Company] as an employer?" (0-10 scale) Promoters (9-10): Calculate as % of total Detractors (0-6): Calculate as % of total NPS = % Promoters - % Detractors Industry Benchmarks: Strong performance: +20 to +40 Excellent performance: +40 to +60 Poor performance: Below 0 Improve NPS by simplifying applications, communicating frequently, setting transparent timelines, and scheduling efficiently . Rejected candidates become referral sources, reapply for roles, and influence others through reviews and social media. Track NPS separately for hired, rejected, and withdrawn candidates. 6. Source of Hire: Optimizing Recruiting Channel Investment Source effectiveness reveals which channels deliver the best candidates at optimal speed and cost. This metric enables data-driven budget allocation across job boards, agencies, referrals, and direct sourcing. Measurement Framework: Track by channel: Volume (applications received) Conversion rates (applications to offers) Time-to-fill by source Cost per hire by channel Quality of hire (90-day performance) High-Performing Channel Indicators: Employee referrals: Highest quality (90%+ retention), lowest cost Direct sourcing: Moderate cost, high quality for technical roles Premium job boards: High volume, moderate quality Agency placements: Fastest fills, highest cost per hire Rehiring former employees (boomerang hires) significantly reduces costs while delivering superior retention. Review source effectiveness quarterly and reallocate budget from low-performing channels. 7. Offer Acceptance Rate: Converting Finalists into Employees Offer acceptance rate measures your ability to close candidates after weeks of recruiting investment. Low rates indicate compensation issues, process problems, or competitor advantages. Formula: (Offers Accepted ÷ Offers Extended) × 100 Industry Benchmarks: Excellent: 85%+ (strong competitive position) Acceptable: 70-84% (room for improvement) Problem indicator: Below 70% (systematic issues) Common Decline Reasons: Non-competitive compensation (42% of declines) Delayed approvals give competitors time (28%) Poor experience during finals (18%) Relocation concerns (12%) Improve acceptance rates by surveying declined candidates, accelerating approval timelines, ensuring market-competitive packages, and maintaining consistent communication. Empower hiring managers to extend offers within 24-48 hours of final interviews. Track acceptance rates by role level and department to identify patterns. 7 Best Practices for Measuring Hiring Effectiveness Having the right KPIs is only half the battle. Successful implementation requires strategic planning, consistent execution, and organizational buy-in. Follow these best practices to transform raw data into actionable recruiting intelligence. Align metrics with business objectives: Select 5-7 KPIs that directly support current business goals. Growth-stage companies prioritize time-to-fill while cost-conscious enterprises focus on efficiency measures, ensuring measurement efforts contribute to organizational success. Establish baselines before setting targets: Collect 3-6 months of historical data to calculate current averages before setting improvement goals, preventing unrealistic targets and identifying which areas need attention (a 65-day baseline tells you exactly how much improvement is required in order to reach your 45-day goal). Apply SMART goals to each KPI: Create Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound objectives, such as "Reduce time-to-fill for engineering roles from 58 to 45 days by Q2 2025", rather than vague objectives that don't drive accountability or change. Document metric definitions for consistency: Maintain uniformity by clearly documenting formulas, data sources, inclusion criteria, and measurement frequency, so your recruiting team calculates metrics consistently and dashboards become trustworthy decision-making tools. Automate data collection through ATS integration: Manual tracking doesn't scale and creates errors at every step. Automate stage transitions, source attribution, and tracking to ensure accurate reporting, so ATS platforms with robust integrations can handle administrative burdens and recruiters can focus on candidate relationships. Build audience-specific dashboards: Design dashboards prioritizing simplicity and visual clarity, tailored for different stakeholders. Executives need high-level KPIs, recruiters need funnel metrics, and hiring managers need quality indicators. Implement structured review cadences: Establish weekly operational check-ins to address immediate bottlenecks, monthly trend analysis to spot patterns, and quarterly strategic assessments to ensure metrics drive decisions rather than sit unused in dashboards. Converting Measurement Insights into Strategic Action Tracking the right metrics provides recruiting leaders with data for strategic decisions. Your time-to-fill average, quality-of-hire score, and Candidate NPS become a common language with finance and executive teams. The difference between successful and struggling recruiting teams comes down to acting on insights. If interview scheduling delays your process, autonomous platforms solve that bottleneck. If technical screening consumes recruiter bandwidth, conversational AI handles initial assessment. Once data shows where the pipeline breaks, deploy the right solution: process redesign, team training, or scalable recruiting technology. Platforms like Alex demonstrate how autonomous AI recruiting works in practice, conducting 5,000+ interviews daily with a 92% candidate rating . Book a demo today to get started. Frequently Asked Questions About Measuring Hiring Effectiveness Q: What are the most critical hiring effectiveness metrics for enterprise recruiting teams? A: Quality of hire, time-to-fill, cost per hire, hiring manager satisfaction, and Candidate Net Promoter Score form the core framework. Quality of hire connects recruiting to business performance through retention and productivity. Track 5-7 KPIs covering quality, speed, cost, and experience. Q: How do I calculate cost per hire to justify recruiting technology investments? Divide total recruiting costs by the number of hires. Industry benchmarks show $1,200-$4,700 for standard roles and $8,750-$35,000 for executive positions. When justifying automation, compare current costs against projected savings from reduced screening, faster fills, preventing revenue loss, improved quality, and lowering replacements. Q: What's a realistic time-to-fill benchmark I should target for my organization? A: Typical ranges are 28-44 days (median) for entry-level and mid-level roles, with executive and specialized positions requiring 60-90 days. Your baseline matters more than industry averages. Measure current performance over the next three months, then set targets that account for your constraints while pushing toward competitive speed. Q: How can I improve offer acceptance rates when competing for top talent? A: Low acceptance rates stem from non-competitive compensation, poor experience, or delayed approvals; survey declining candidates to identify patterns. Accelerate approvals with pre-approved salary bands, improve communication during finals, ensure market-competitive packages, and empower managers to extend offers within 24-48 hours. Q: Why should enterprise recruiting teams measure candidate experience for rejected applicants? A: Candidate NPS impacts employer brand regardless of outcomes. Rejected candidates become referral sources, reapply, or influence others via social media. Strong brands report NPS scores of +30 to +50 among rejected candidates, reducing cost per hire by increasing applications and strengthening referrals.

NON-GAAP FINANCIAL MEASURES AND RECONCILIATION TO GAAP NET INCOME The Company has four primary variables that impact its performance: (i) net interest margin on assets held within the investment portfolio; (ii) realized and unrealized gains or losses on assets held within the investment portfolio and operating companies, including any impairment or reserve for expected credit losses; (iii) income from the Company’s operating company investments; and (iv) the Company’s operating expenses and taxes. “Earnings available for distribution” is a non-GAAP financial measure of the Company’s operating performance, which is used by management to evaluate the Company’s performance, excluding: (i) net realized and unrealized gains and losses on certain assets and liabilities; (ii) net other income and losses; (iii) non-capitalized transaction-related expenses; (iv) depreciation and amortization on real estate investment properties; (v) straight-line rental income on commercial real estate properties; and (vi) deferred taxes. The Company’s definition of earnings available for distribution excludes certain realized and unrealized losses, which although they represent a part of the Company’s recurring operations, are subject to significant variability and are generally limited to a potential indicator of future economic performance. Within net other income and losses, management primarily excludes (i) equity-based compensation expenses, (ii) non-cash deferred interest expense, (iii) amortization expense related to intangible assets and debt acquired below or above market prices and (iv) straight-line rental income on commercial real estate properties, as management does not consider this non-cash activity to be a component of earnings available for distribution. With regard to non-capitalized transaction-related expenses, management does not view these costs as part of the Company’s core operations, as they are considered by management to be similar to realized losses incurred at acquisition. Non-capitalized transaction related expenses generally relate to legal and valuation service costs, as well as other professional service fees, incurred when the Company acquires certain investments, as well as costs associated with the acquisition and integration of acquired businesses. Management also excludes deferred taxes because the Company believes deferred taxes are not representative of current operations. Management believes that the adjustments to compute “earnings available for distribution” specified above allow investors and analysts to readily identify and track the operating performance of the assets that form the core of the Company’s activity, assist in comparing the core operating results between periods and enable investors to evaluate the Company’s current core performance using the same financial measure that management uses to operate the business. Management also utilizes earnings available for distribution as a financial measure in its decision-making process relating to improvements to the underlying fundamental operations of the Company’s investments, as well as the allocation of resources between those investments, and management also relies on earnings available for distribution as an indicator of the results of such decisions. Earnings available for distribution excludes certain recurring items, such as gains and losses (including impairment and reserves as well as derivative activities) and non-capitalized transaction-related expenses, because they are not considered by management to be part of the Company’s core operations for the reasons described herein. As such, earnings available for distribution is not intended to reflect all of the Company’s activity and should be considered as only one of the factors used by management in assessing the Company’s performance, along with GAAP net income which is inclusive of all of the Company’s activities. The Company views earnings available for distribution as a consistent financial measure of its portfolio’s ability to generate income for distribution to common stockholders. Earnings available for distribution does not represent and should not be considered as a substitute for, or superior to, net income or as a substitute for, or superior to, cash flows from operating activities, each as determined in accordance with GAAP, and the Company’s calculation of this financial measure may not be comparable to similarly entitled financial measures reported by other companies. title: The Modalities of Tap to pay in Africa
summary: The emergence of Tap to Pay in Africa is a symbol of the rapid adoption of digital finance. Especially in Nigeria, where electronic tra...
body_text: The emergence of Tap to Pay in Africa is a symbol of the rapid adoption of digital finance. Especially in Nigeria, where electronic transactions reached ₦295 trillion ($295B+) in the first quarter of 2025 alone, reflecting over 20% year-on-year growth. Contactless cards aren’t just a western trend; it's gradually becoming the African standard. From the busy streets of Lagos to the shopping marts of Johannesburg, "tap to pay" is reshaping consumer expectations. But for enterprises looking to implement this technology across the continent, understanding the nuances is critical to building a scalable and reliable payment infrastructure. In this article, you’ll learn how tap to pay works, its market regulations, and how to choose the right card issuer for your business. What is Tap to Pay? At its core, tap to pay is a contactless method for customers to complete purchases. Instead of swiping or inserting a card, consumers simply hold their card, smartphone, or wearable device near a payment terminal. The magic behind this convenience is Near-Field Communication (NFC) , a short-range wireless technology that allows two devices (like a card and a terminal) to communicate securely when they are just a few centimeters apart. It’s helpful to distinguish between the common terms: Tap to Pay refers to the process a consumer follows to complete a payment transaction. Contactless payment is the broader category of payments that don't require physical contact. NFC is the underlying technology that powers the tap. The Three Primary Modalities of Tap to Pay In the African market, enterprises must be equipped to handle three common ways customers tap to pay. 1. Contactless Cards These are traditional debit or credit cards embedded with an NFC chip and antenna, that replaces the magnetic stripe or chip insertion with a simple tap. As of early 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria reported over 12 million contactless cards in circulation nationwide. Regionally, major African payment brands like Verve have issued more than 30 million contactless cards, with additional adoption growing steadily across other financial institutions 2. Mobile Wallets (Smartphones) Smartphones have become the central hub for modern life, and payments are no exception. Major mobile wallets like Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Samsung Pay allow customers to load their card information securely onto their devices. Currently, there are over 1 billion registered mobile money wallets in Africa, accounting for roughly 53% of all mobile money wallets worldwide and over 70% of the total global transaction value. 3. Wearable Payments Although this method isn’t popular in Africa, NFC-enabled smartwatches (Apple Watch, Samsung Galaxy Watch), fitness trackers (Garmin Pay, Fitbit Pay), and even payment rings and wristbands are gaining traction worldwide. The global market for these devices is projected to reach $82 billion by 2026, and they offer a frictionless experience for consumers who prefer not to pull out a phone or card. Read also - Payment Tokenizations: What it is and How it Works Regulations & Use Cases of Tap to Pay in Africa For enterprises building on Miden's infrastructure, navigating local regulations is as important as understanding the technology itself. The regulatory environment across Africa continues to evolve to encourage and secure contactless adoption. South Africa leads adoption, with over 50% of urban card transactions now NFC enabled. Contactless payments at fuel stations and Quick Service Restaurants (QSRs) grew from 42% in 2023 to 53% in 2024. In Nigeria, CBN guidelines limit single transactions to ₦15,000 and daily transactions to ₦50,000. Transactions above the limit require PIN/biometric verification and must route through NIBSS. Despite limits, contactless payment still holds a large user share in public transportation via Cowrywise's NFC cards. Kenya & East Africa’s contactless standards are integrating with established mobile money ecosystems like M-Pesa, creating hybrid payment models unique to the region. Morocco and Ivory Coast have digitized over 20,000 neighborhood shops respectively, equipping street vendors with NFC payment tools. Miden is the financial operating system for modern businesses and enterprises. From card issuing to global payments, pay-ins & pay-outs, plus an AI-driven core banking engine, our composable, API-first infrastructure gives you the tools to launch and scale with confidence. Built in Africa. Designed for the world. Learn more Barriers and Challenges Even with the promise of quicker and safer transactions, Africa is still a long way from full adoption and here are some reasons: Hardware Constraints : Currently, only about 24%–25% of the Sub-Saharan African population actually owns an NFC enabled smartphone. This makes tap to pay integration very difficult to achieve. Connectivity Issues : The prevalence of network downtime and unstable power supply which affects both user and merchant, reduces the possibilities of contactless payments. Low Trust and Awareness: User trust remains a key hurdle for contactless adoption, with many customers preferring the familiarity of traditional payment methods. How Miden Provides Corporate Cards For Enterprises Building a financial product that seamlessly supports all these modalities requires stitching together various infrastructure. One provider for card issuance, another for mobile wallets, another for compliance. Miden simplifies this. Our platform powers card issuing, accruals, disbursements, and global payments—all through a single API integration. With Miden Tap-to-Pay, your business can immediately enable contactless payments without managing multiple providers. Our Tap to pay is: Enabled for Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Samsung Pay. Built on the tokenization principles that keep the PAN out of the payment flow. The card networks generate a device-specific token that replaces the PAN for every transaction. Equipped to handle unforeseen events. If a user loses their phone, they simply log in on a new device, and the card reconstitutes itself, reducing support tickets and ensuring a positive end-user experience. For African enterprises searching for cross-border market opportunities, the possibilities are endless. Contactless payments are the future, and with Miden as your infrastructure partner, you can scale above competitors, and build for whatever comes next. To get started, new businesses can reach out to our sales team to be onboarded while existing customers can upgrade their card programs directly from the Miden dashboard. title: What is BYOC?
summary: A practical guide to Bring Your Own Cloud — what it is, why enterprises demand it, and what it takes to deliver it
body_text: Ever since ChatGPT launched in late 2022, enterprise software procurement has structurally shifted. Security teams that once sat at the back of the process now gate purchasing decisions with decisive power. Data-sensitive systems built on centralized architectures are increasingly getting blocked at the CISO's desk. This isn't slowing down. Every application now handles more sensitive data than it did a year ago, as LLMs lowered the barrier to incorporating unstructured information into practical workflows—expanding the surface area of sensitive data exposure. The same language models also reduce the cost of exploitation. The time required to operationalize a CVE compressed from weeks to hours. On-prem / self-hosted deployments were supposed to be the solution. In practice, they introduce an untenable set of constraints — months to get a customer live, cloud/Kubernetes hell, a dedicated engineer to keep it running, and no way to push patches without involving the customer's operations team. That reputation exists for a reason. BYOC — Bring Your Own Cloud — emerged instead. Your software runs in the customer's cloud, while preserving your control over the release cycle. It works when it's done right. Getting there is the hard part. What BYOC actually means Your software runs inside your customer's cloud account instead of yours. They provide the infrastructure — their AWS, Azure, or GCP account — and you deploy and manage the application within it. You already know the two models on either side of it. SaaS: you host everything, customer data comes to you. Simple, until a customer with a security team tells you that's not happening. On-prem: you ship them Docker images and Helm charts and lose control. You don't know what version they're running. You can't push a patch. If something breaks at 2am, you're waiting for their ops team to wake up. BYOC sits between the two. Your app runs in their cloud, so their security team signs off. But you still own the release cycle. You push updates, you monitor health, you roll back when something breaks. Their data never crosses the boundary. You never SSH into their boxes. Why enterprises keep asking for it When a multi-tenant SaaS vendor gets breached, every customer on that platform is exposed at once. And this keeps happening. Third party vendor compromises are 14% of all breaches now. Average cost in the US: $10.22 million. Then there's compliance. HIPAA, SOC 2, FedRAMP, GDPR, DORA — the acronyms keep multiplying but they all come down to roughly the same thing: keep sensitive data inside the customer's boundary. With BYOC that's just how it works. The data never leaves. There's also a financial argument. If you're a product that move a lot of data — like ClickHouse, Grafana, or Databricks — your enterprise customers are paying enormous egress fees. Deploy in their cloud and that egress bill goes to zero. And for compute heavy products, enterprises can instead spend against their existing cloud commit. Why isn't everyone doing BYOC then? It's hard. We spent years on this problem at Palantir, building the deployment platform that manages over 300 environments spread across AWS, GCP, Azure, and bare metal on-prem. Traditional SaaS lets you manage one environment with one set of tools. BYOC means you're managing dozens or hundreds of isolated environments, each in a different cloud account with different network configurations and security policies. Provisioning alone is painful: spinning up Kubernetes clusters, databases, networking, and IAM roles inside cloud accounts you don't control. What works in one account might fail in another because of a service quota or org level policy you didn't know existed. Updates are worse. You push whenever you want in SaaS, but with BYOC you're coordinating releases across environments that might each be on a different version. Rolling back one customer without touching the others takes more orchestration than most teams expect. And then you need to debug issues in environments you can't SSH into, using monitoring tools that assume you own the infrastructure. Even the first BYOC deployment is a project. Before you can put anything in a customer's cloud, you need production-grade Helm charts, Terraform modules for their provider, Docker images built for their architecture, and IAM policies that satisfy their security team. Most of this didn't exist in your SaaS stack because you never needed it. Now you're building deployment infrastructure from scratch while also trying to ship product. By the second customer, you're spending engineering time maintaining those stacks alongside the customer. By the third or fourth, you've got multiple versions of your product in flight and everything gets worse at once. Which customer is on which version? Why is this one throwing errors the others aren't? You can't easily pull telemetry from systems you don't own, so debugging turns into archaeology. Every stack starts feeling like a snowflake. You've probably deployed across multiple cloud providers by now too, which is its own problem. By ten it's consuming a serious chunk of your engineering resources. You only get to a hundred if you've figured out how to automate the deployment factory. This is why so many vendors either refuse BYOC deals or charge a huge premium and throw bodies at the problem. How it works in practice The architecture is simpler than you'd expect. You run a management plane on your side. It doesn't touch customer data. All it does is decide what goes where. Which customer gets which version, when to push an update. Inside each customer's cloud there's a lightweight control plane that picks up those decisions and executes them. Deploys Helm charts, runs Terraform, rotates secrets, reports back on health. All communication is outbound. The control plane calls home to you. You never reach into their environment. No open ports, no VPN tunnels, no standing credentials. Getting a new customer on takes minutes. They run a provisioning template in their cloud account, it spins up a cluster with the control plane installed, and it connects back. That's the whole onboarding. When you actually need it Not every product needs this. If you're selling a project management tool to 50-person startups, SaaS is fine and you should stick with it. But if your customers handle healthcare records, financial transactions, classified information, or PII, and they can't let that data leave their environment, BYOC is the way to do it. Security teams with veto power over vendor selection will actually talk to you instead of just saying no. Prospects who keep asking for self-hosted get a yes without the operational nightmare. And these customers routinely pay multiples of the standard SaaS price. They're paying for control and compliance, and they expect to. Build or buy If you build it yourself, the list is long. Terraform modules for every cloud. A control plane. A management plane. Observability that works across environments you don't own. An upgrade system that doesn't break when one customer is three versions behind another. Some teams pull this off, but it usually takes 3 to 5 engineers for most of a year, and then someone has to maintain it. That might make sense if BYOC is your core product. If it's a delivery mechanism for your actual product, that's a lot of engineering going somewhere other than your core competency. Or you use a platform that's already solved this. You hand it your Helm charts, Terraform modules, Docker images, or just point it at the code in your repo, tell it how things should be deployed, and it does the rest, across AWS, GCP, Azure, wherever your customers are. How to tell if a BYOC implementation is any good After seeing enough of these you start to notice what separates the ones that work. Onboarding speed is the first tell. If it takes days to get a customer live, the architecture is probably wrong. After that it's mostly security questions. Do you hold persistent credentials to their cloud? Can you update one customer without touching the others? Does any data leave their VPC? Is every action logged? Buyers who want BYOC know to ask all of these. Get one wrong and they walk. What happens next Ten years ago the security question around SaaS was mostly theoretical. The industry was moving to the cloud and nobody worried much about where data lived. That changed. Breaches got bigger and more frequent. The attack surface of a centralized multi-tenant system grows every year. We built Ryvn because we think that trend doesn't reverse. Something changed in the last year. Someone finds a CVE, feeds it to an LLM, and has a working exploit by the end of the day. That used to take a specialist weeks. The security teams on the other side of your deals have noticed, even if most vendors haven't. There's a second LLM effect that matters more for BYOC. A year ago most of the unstructured data in your customers' environments — documents, conversations, logs, support tickets — just sat there. Now you can actually do something with it. Feed it into your product against your business logic and the thing gets dramatically more useful. Every vendor is going to build those integrations. It's too obvious not to. Which means you're pulling in more of your customer's data than ever. At some point they're going to look at that and say, just run the software over here. For a lot of industries that's already happening. Software is going to move to where data already lives, and BYOC is how.

body_text: 87 percent reduction in risk of death compared to patients who received placebo (hazard ratio: 0.13, p-value: < 0.0001) REDWOOD CITY, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Apr. 30, 2026-- Corcept Therapeutics Incorporated (NASDAQ: CORT), a commercial-stage company engaged in the discovery and development of medications to treat severe endocrinologic, oncologic, metabolic and neurologic disorders by modulating the effects of the hormone cortisol, today announced two-year overall survival data from the Phase 2 DAZALS study of its proprietary, selective cortisol modulator dazucorilant in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). DAZALS is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2 study in which 249 patients with ALS were randomized to receive either 150 mg of dazucorilant, 300 mg of dazucorilant or placebo, daily for 24 weeks. Patients who completed the treatment period were eligible to enter the study’s long-term extension phase, in which all patients received 300 mg of dazucorilant. DAZAL’s primary endpoint was the difference in function, as measured by the ALS Functional Rating Scale – Revised (ALSFRS-R), between patients who received dazucorilant and those who received placebo. Overall survival was a secondary endpoint. Although DAZALS did not meet its primary endpoint, at the end of the 24-week treatment period patients who received 300 mg of dazucorilant daily did exhibit improved overall survival (p-value: 0.02). Exploratory analyses show that this survival benefit has continued. In the two years following the start of treatment, patients who received 300 mg of dazucorilant experienced an 87 percent reduction in the risk of death compared to patients who received placebo and did not switch to 300 mg of dazucorilant in the extension phase (hazard ratio: 0.13; p-value: < 0.0001). This finding is consistent with the 84 percent reduction in risk of death observed after one year of treatment (hazard ratio: 0.16; p-value: 0.0009). Those one-year data were presented at the European Network to Cure ALS (ENCALS) 2025 annual meeting. A similarly pronounced survival benefit was observed at both the one-year and two-year marks in patients who received 300 mg of dazucorilant for more than 24 weeks, whether in the treatment period or in the long-term extension phase, compared to patients who received either placebo or 150 mg of dazucorilant for more than 24 weeks and did not receive dazucorilant in the extension phase. Between these groups, the reduction in risk of death in patients who received 300 mg of dazucorilant was 64 percent at one year (hazard ratio: 0.36; p-value: 0.02) and 61 percent at two years (hazard ratio: 0.39; p-value: 0.02). Dazucorilant continues to demonstrate an acceptable safety profile, with mild to moderate, dose-related, transient abdominal pain being the most common adverse effect. Corcept is conducting a dose titration study to refine methods of improving dazucorilant’s gastrointestinal tolerability and inform the program’s path forward. “Our data demonstrate that dazucorilant markedly reduces mortality in the first years following diagnosis, when people with ALS retain meaningful function and quality of life,” said Bill Guyer, PharmD, Corcept’s Chief Development Officer. “We are working with regulators to advance this program as expeditiously as possible and expect to initiate a pivotal Phase 3 study later this year.” About the DAZALS Study DAZALS is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2 trial in which 249 patients with ALS were randomized 1:1:1 to receive either 150 mg of dazucorilant, 300 mg of dazucorilant or placebo daily for 24 weeks. Patients who completed the treatment period were eligible to enroll in the study’s long-term extension phase, in which all patients received 300 mg of dazucorilant. Baseline patient characteristics, including the ENCALS risk score, time from diagnosis, ALSFRS-R total score, and bulbar onset, were consistent across study arms. The DAZALS primary endpoint was the difference in change from baseline during the study’s 24-week treatment period in ALSFRS-R score between patients who received dazucorilant and those who received placebo. Key secondary endpoints include overall survival and quality of life. DAZALS was conducted at sites in Europe, the United States and Canada. About Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease or motor neuron disease, is a fatal degenerative neurologic disorder that affects more than 55,000 people in the United States and Europe. ALS causes muscles to weaken and, as the disease progresses, severely impairs patients’ ability to speak, eat, move and breathe. There is increasing evidence that patients with ALS, particularly those with rapid disease progression, exhibit elevated or abnormal cortisol levels. A patient’s life expectancy after diagnosis is two to five years. About Dazucorilant Dazucorilant is a selective cortisol modulator that binds to the glucocorticoid receptor but not to the body’s other hormone receptors. Corcept is studying dazucorilant as a potential treatment for ALS and other neurologic disorders. The compound is proprietary to Corcept and is protected by composition of matter, method of use and other patents. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has granted dazucorilant Fast Track Designation and orphan drug status for the treatment of ALS in the United States. About Corcept Therapeutics For over 25 years, Corcept has focused on cortisol modulation and its potential to treat patients with a wide variety of serious disorders and has discovered more than 1,000 proprietary selective cortisol modulators and glucocorticoid receptor antagonists. Corcept is conducting advanced clinical trials in patients with Cushing’s syndrome, solid tumors, ALS and liver disease. In 2012, the company introduced Korlym®, the first medication approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of patients with endogenous Cushing’s syndrome, and in 2026, the company introduced Lifyorli™, approved in combination with nab-paclitaxel, the first FDA-approved selective glucocorticoid receptor antagonist, for adults with platinum-resistant ovarian cancer. Corcept is headquartered in Redwood City, California. For more information, visit Corcept.com . title: How the ‘Hannah Montana 20th Anniversary Special’ Was Produced by Fans for Fans
summary: Disney employees who were inspired by 'Hannah Montana' as kids detail their work to bring the anniversary special to life.
body_text: How the ‘Hannah Montana 20th Anniversary Special’ Was Produced by Fans for Fans Entertainment April 23, 2026 7 min. read According to Disney Legend Miley Cyrus, she manifested the Hannah Montana 20th Anniversary Special well before Disney Branded Television gave it the official greenlight. “One of my favorite pieces of advice [Dolly Parton] ever gave me was, ‘Start promoting something before it’s real, because then as people get excited, it’ll be easier to make it happen,’” Cyrus said in an interview with ABC’s Good Morning America . “I just started talking about a Hannah-versary special before one even existed — and then I went to Disney and said, ‘Look how excited everyone is about this imaginary Hannah-versary!’” After Hannah Montana premiered on Disney Channel in 2006, the EmmyⓇ-nominated series spawned 14 platinum and 18 gold albums worldwide, as well as two feature films. Proving the franchise’s long-lasting popularity, the Hannah Montana catalog has amassed more than half a billion hours streamed globally on Disney+ to date. And, following its March 24 premiere on Disney+ and Hulu, The Hannah Montana 20th Anniversary Special notched 6.3 million views in just three days of streaming. Proving fans couldn’t get enough, the entire Hannah Montana catalog saw a near 1,000% increase in views that week. ( Click here for more stats about the anniversary special’s performance.) Now Streaming Now Available Disney Legend Miley Cyrus returns home to celebrate the ‘Hannah Montana’ 20th anniversary. 2026 Watch on Disney+ “You’ll Always Find Your Way Back Home” The Hannah Montana 20th Anniversary Special marked a full-circle moment — and not just for Cyrus. Some of the show’s biggest fans are Cast Members and employees at The Walt Disney Company. In fact, several attended the anniversary special’s taping at Sunset Gower Studios in Hollywood, dressing up in outfits inspired by the fictional pop star as Cyrus performed “ This Is the Life ” and “ The Climb ,” two of her character’s signature songs. “Disney is first in class when it comes to fan affinity, so we weaved that fan-first approach throughout every aspect of the campaign,” said Leah Palacios, Manager, Publicity, Disney Branded Television (DBT), who helped lead the PR campaign, attended the taping, and worked the premiere event. Palacios recalled, “The ability to tap that childlike joy within people through the content we create and opportunities we provide is truly unique to Disney and I feel grateful to have a career that allows me to share that magic with others.” Sydney Holt, Then and Now Not only did Joshua Jack Ryan Maddela, Coordinator, Events, Disney Entertainment Television (DET), attend the taping, but he helped plan and work at the premiere event. “I am such a huge fan of the series, so it was such a treat to dive into the premiere research,” Maddela said. “I rewatched some of my favorite episodes to take notes on everything from iconic quotes to outfits. During the planning process, you would often find me listening to a Hannah Montana music Spotify playlist on repeat in my cubicle. Some of the ways we incorporated our research were working with our amazing Walt Disney Archives team to select iconic props from the series and movie to display. Our team incorporated foods such as Rico’s Empanadas and Sweet Niblets Elote to give a nod to the original series. Our team wanted to ensure that guests at the premiere knew it was an event for Hannah Montana fans made by Hannah Montana fans!” For those who produced and promoted the anniversary special, seeing Cyrus revisit her legendary role was a dream come true — and something that only Disney could pull off. “Attending the taping felt like giving something to my kid-self,” said Brynn Candle, Coordinator, Original Movies, DBT. “It is rare that you get to be around so many people that love something that means so much to you, especially while wearing a wig. Being able to sing my heart out with an entire room of fans was honestly like nothing I have experienced before. It was a homecoming for Miley, but it also felt like a homecoming for all of us.” Fabiola Megaptche, Sr. Executive Assistant, Publicity, DET, said it was “unbelievable”” to work the premiere and attend the taping. “The energy in the room was incredible, and you could tell it was a special moment for everyone,” she said. “If you told 7-year-old me that I would see Hannah Montana live, she would’ve burst into tears — and 23-year-old me did!” Our team wanted to ensure that guests at the premiere knew it was an event for Hannah Montana fans made by Hannah Montana fans! — Jack Ryan Maddela, Coordinator, Events, DET “Life’s What You Make It” On March 23, Cyrus reunited with original series stars Jason Earles, Moises Arias, Cody Linley, Anna Maria Perez de Tagle, and Shanica Knowles when she walked the purple carpet at the premiere of Hannah Montana 20th Anniversary Special at the El Capitan Theatre — the same venue where Hannah Montana: The Movie held its premiere in 2009. “Out of the many red carpets I’ve worked, this one was truly something special,” said Kayla Martin, Manager, Visual Communications, DET. “The energy was electric, from the attendees’ incredible Hannah‑inspired outfits to the shared sense of nostalgia and collective understanding that we were all part of something meaningful… What stood out most to me was the sense of community. Seeing coworkers, talent, influencers, and longtime fans come together to fangirl, reminisce, and celebrate Hannah Montana through this special felt like I was a part of a cultural moment. It was rare and special to witness so many people connected by the same joy.” Kayla Martin, Then and Now Then, on March 24 — exactly 20 years after Hannah Montana premiered on Disney Channel — employees from Burbank and Chicago to San Antonio and New York City celebrated the milestone anniversary at surprise pop-ups that included themed photo-ops, collectible giveaways, and more. And many of the fans Hannah Montana inspired now work alongside its creators to shape the next chapter of Disney Branded Television storytelling. Like High School Musical and other phenomena of that era, Hannah Montana was about “showing up as your authentic self and being part of a community,” Sydney Holt, St. Executive Assistant, Live Action & Alternative Series, DBT, added. “Those themes connect us as employees and continue to guide the stories we’re telling today.” Leroy Marshall, Then and Now Likewise, Nancy Insua, Manager, Publicity, DBT, recalled how the classic Hannah Montana song “ I’ve Got Nerve ” gave her “so much confidence as a kid” — confidence she carried into adulthood. Today, she feels a personal affinity to the stories she helps promote. “There’s always a connection to the content you can tap into. My family watched together, and knowing families continue to have those experiences today is incredibly meaningful.” Leroy Marshall, Executive Assistant, Content & Inclusion, DBT, had a similar story. “Hannah Montana always had a confidence to her that I dreamed of when I was a kid,” he said. “Attending the taping felt like a dream come true, and took me right back to 9-year-old Leroy, who had the craziest dreams of the world and always prayed that one day I’d reach them!” Related Tags Streaming Disney Entertainment Television Follow Us LinkedIn Facebook YouTube

(NYSE American LLC: CCEL ) (the “Company”), the world’s first private cord blood bank to separate and store stem cells in 1992, announced results for the fiscal first quarter ended February 28, 2026. Financial Results Revenue The revenues for the first quarter of fiscal 2026 were $7.68 million compared to $7.97 million for the first quarter of fiscal 2025. The revenues for the first quarter of fiscal 2026 consisted of $7.64 million in processing and storage fee revenue, $36,000 in product revenue and approximately $1,400 in public banking revenue compared to $7.87 million in processing and storage fee revenue, $21,000 in product revenue and approximately $82,000 in public banking revenue for the first quarter of fiscal 2025. About Cryo-Cell International, Inc. Founded in 1989, Cryo-Cell International, Inc. is the world’s first private cord blood bank. ‎ The Company currently stores over 250,000 cord blood and cord tissue specimens for the exclusive benefit of newborn babies and possibly other members of their families. In addition to its private bank, Cryo-Cell ‎International, Inc. has a public banking program in partnership with Duke University. Cryo-Cell’s ‎public bank has provided cord blood for more than 700 transplants and operates a cord ‎blood donation site at one of the country’s most prominent hospitals, Cedars–Sinai Hospital in ‎Los Angeles. title: How to Migrate from Storyblok to Cosmic
summary: A step-by-step guide for developers migrating from Storyblok to Cosmic: content model mapping, component-to-metafield conversion, media migration, API migration, and webhooks — with real TypeScript code examples.
body_text: Why Developers Are Migrating from Storyblok to Cosmic Storyblok was a smart choice for teams who wanted a visual editor baked into their CMS. But as applications grow in complexity and AI becomes central to content operations, its limitations become harder to work around. Three pain points keep coming up in migration conversations: Visual editor lock-in. Storyblok components are built around page presentation, which couples your content model to your frontend. When you need to reuse content across channels, that coupling becomes a bottleneck. Pricing pressure. Seat fees, delivery limits, and add-on costs compound as teams grow. Budgeting for Storyblok at scale is unpredictable. No native AI. Adding AI to a Storyblok workflow requires third-party integrations and significant custom engineering. Cosmic has AI Agents built in. If any of those sound familiar, this guide will walk you through the full migration process: content model mapping, component-to-metafield conversion, media migration, API migration, and webhooks. Before You Start: Understanding the Key Differences Storyblok Concept Cosmic Equivalent Story Object Component/Block Object Type + Metafields Component Field Metafield Space Bucket Asset Media Datasource Object Type (for structured reference data) Webhook Webhook (via add-on) The most important conceptual shift: Storyblok organizes content around components on stories . Cosmic organizes content around Objects of a given Object Type . The result is more flexible — you're not constrained by what a visual editor can preview. Step 1: Map Your Content Model Start by auditing your Storyblok components. For each component, you'll create a corresponding Object Type in Cosmic with the right Metafields. Storyblok Component → Cosmic Object Type If you have a Storyblok component like this: // Storyblok: Blog Post component { "name" : "blog_post" , "display_name" : "Blog Post" , "schema" : { "title" : { "type" : "text" } , "body" : { "type" : "richtext" } , "author" : { "type" : "text" } , "published_date" : { "type" : "datetime" } , "featured_image" : { "type" : "asset" } } } Your Cosmic Object Type would look like: // Cosmic: Blog Post Object Type (created via dashboard or API) { title : 'Blog Posts' , slug : 'blog-posts' , metafields : [ { key : 'title' , title : 'Title' , type : 'text' } , { key : 'body' , title : 'Body' , type : 'markdown' } , { key : 'author' , title : 'Author' , type : 'text' } , { key : 'published_date' , title : 'Published Date' , type : 'date' } , { key : 'featured_image' , title : 'Featured Image' , type : 'file' } ] } Tips for the mapping process: Storyblok richtext → Cosmic markdown or html-textarea Storyblok asset → Cosmic file Storyblok multiasset → Cosmic files Storyblok option (single select) → Cosmic select Storyblok options (multi select) → Cosmic multi-select Storyblok nested blocks → Cosmic objects relationship field or repeater Storyblok story reference → Cosmic object relationship field Step 2: Export Your Content from Storyblok Use the Storyblok Management API to export your stories. You'll need your Storyblok API token. // export-storyblok.ts import fetch from 'node-fetch' const STORYBLOK_TOKEN = process . env . STORYBLOK_TOKEN const STORYBLOK_SPACE_ID = process . env . STORYBLOK_SPACE_ID async function exportStories ( page = 1 , allStories : any [ ] = [ ] ) : Promise < any [ ] > { const res = await fetch ( ` https://mapi.storyblok.com/v1/spaces/ ${ STORYBLOK_SPACE_ID } /stories/?per_page=100&page= ${ page } ` , { headers : { Authorization : STORYBLOK_TOKEN as string } } ) const data = await res . json ( ) as { stories : any [ ] , total : number } const stories = data . stories || [ ] allStories . push ( ... stories ) const total = parseInt ( res . headers . get ( 'total' ) || '0' ) const fetched = allStories . length if ( fetched < total ) { return exportStories ( page + 1 , allStories ) } return allStories } exportStories ( ) . then ( stories => { console . log ( ` Exported ${ stories . length } stories ` ) // Write to JSON file for import step const fs = require ( 'fs' ) fs . writeFileSync ( 'storyblok-export.json' , JSON . stringify ( stories , null , 2 ) ) } ) Step 3: Migrate Media Assets Before importing content objects, migrate your media. Storyblok stores assets on their CDN; you'll need to re-upload them to Cosmic's media library. // migrate-media.ts import { createBucketClient } from '@cosmicjs/sdk' const cosmic = createBucketClient ( { bucketSlug : process . env . COSMIC_BUCKET_SLUG as string , readKey : process . env . COSMIC_READ_KEY as string , writeKey : process . env . COSMIC_WRITE_KEY as string } ) function mapStoryToCosmicObject ( story : any ) { const { content } = story // Replace Storyblok asset URLs with Cosmic URLs function replaceAssetUrls ( obj : any ) : any { if ( ! obj || typeof obj !== 'object' ) return obj if ( typeof obj === 'string' && assetMap [ obj ] ) return assetMap [ obj ] if ( Array . isArray ( obj ) ) return obj . map ( replaceAssetUrls ) return Object . fromEntries ( Object . entries ( obj ) . map ( ( [ k , v ] ) => [ k , replaceAssetUrls ( v ) ] ) ) } const mappedContent = replaceAssetUrls ( content ) return { title : story . name , slug : story . slug , type : 'blog-posts' , // Change to match your Object Type slug status : story . published ? COSMIC_BUCKET_SLUG } /objects? ` + new URLSearchParams ( { query : JSON . stringify ( { type : 'blog-posts' } ) , props : 'title,slug,metadata,published_at' , read_key : process . env . COSMIC_READ_KEY as string , status : 'published' } ) ) const { objects : posts } = await response . json ( ) Using the Cosmic JavaScript/TypeScript SDK // After: Cosmic SDK (recommended) import { createBucketClient } from '@cosmicjs/sdk' const cosmic = createBucketClient ( { bucketSlug : process . env . body_text: Today, we released a major update to how Repaint generates websites. It can follow more specific instructions, and it's more flexible when redesigning sites. Major improvements: It can rebuild a website in its original style. It's better at using other sites as references. It can generate custom styles, outside the premade gallery. Repaint was originally built to fully redesign sites in a new style. We realized redesigning a website is rarely all-or-nothing. Sometimes you want to preserve the original site, sometimes you want a full redesign, and often you want something in between. With this update, Repaint is much better at handling all of it. You can try the new system live in Repaint today.

Speeding AI Deployment Through Simplified and Accelerated Validation
summary: Testing traffic emulation, performance benchmarking and flow-level analytics help create reliable AI-ready systems.
body_text: Speeding AI Deployment Through Simplified and Accelerated Validation Ed Nakamoto April 28, 2026 2 The workloads of today’s artificial intelligence (AI) applications place extraordinary demands on the quality and reliability of high-speed networks. That is true during AI training or inferencing to respond to the growing number of users issuing complex prompts, but the two broad usage models have significantly different requirements than the network connecting the thousands of computing nodes. Each brings its own complications to making a data-center network ready for AI. In the case of training, the network must support efficient, high-bandwidth data transfers with low latency and offer tight synchronization between the nodes. Training communication frequently entails bursts of all-to-all traffic as each node broadcasts new weight values to their peers at the end of a batch of calculations. Because training cannot continue without all the parallel sub-tasks completing successfully, it demands lossless connectivity and low latency even under intense bursts of activity. Training is not unique in its need for low latency. Inferencing requires minimal network delays to minimize the waiting time for clients. But the traffic patterns differ greatly from those found in training runs, with the network needing to serve many requests that come from outside the network as new prompts and data arrive, and also internally from the reasoning chains of “thinking” models. This is particularly the case in the new generation of large-scale mixture-of-expert systems. AI Data Center Fabric Testing Requirements Techniques such as load balancing to reduce bottlenecks and elastic scaling of infrastructure are vital to maintaining quality-of-service guarantees and high accelerator or GPU utilization on each computing node. A further requirement for inferencing is the need to enforce much higher levels of security and traffic monitoring because of the danger of mass attacks on AI models. How training and inference suffer from network problems can differ dramatically. For example, a 2023 analysis of training tasks by Alibaba and Nanjing University found that less than 60% of them succeeded on the first attempt. Of those that failed, almost half were because of errors associated with the network. Important protocols developed to help implement distributed processing, such as the Collective Communications Library (CCL), employ timeouts to avoid operations becoming deadlocked. But timeouts stemming from congestion can lead to individual tasks failing. That proved to be the leading network-related factor in task failures in the study. In addition, errors such as link flapping , where network ports were intermittently available, caused a significant number of those network failures. These errors underline the necessity for a holistic approach to network validation and testing for operators. Link flapping, for example, rarely stems from a single-layer problem. Rather it often arises from conflicting interactions between automatic optical protection and IP settings, which trigger an oscillation where links switch rapidly between active to inactive states. In the inferencing environment, traffic patterns are far less predictable. Bursts of user activity can easily lead to congestion. This results in blocked transactions that may drive a cascade of negative effects that reduce throughput across a large part of the data center. Many systems will also be vulnerable to attacks that aim at denial of service, or which attempt to compromise AI agents at the prompt level. Operators need to examine how many different scenarios will affect the network in addition to analyzing how well the network architecture distributes work to the nodes across the data center to maximize utilization and profitability. High-Speed Ethernet in AI Data Centers Operators are turning to novel forms of high-speed Ethernet to help deal with the requirements of AI traffic, which focus on techniques to reduce latency by reducing the number of handshake transactions needed for connections and improvements to congestion control. Data centers may use combinations of conventional Ethernet equipment and switches that handle newer protocols like Ultra Ethernet. It will therefore be vital to ensure these systems coexist seamlessly and to identify where paths might benefit from upgrades. The migration from InfiniBand to Ethernet in AI back-end networks. (Source: Dell’Oro Group) The key to handling these issues is to perform extensive validation of the network architecture and equipment used, from the physical layer up to high-level packet control. But at the scale that AI training and inferencing systems now encompass, achieving the levels of traffic required to perform extensive testing requires the test framework to be built around the many individual tests required. Some scenarios require emulation of GPUs, accelerators, and data-processing units (xPUs) to generate large amounts of inter-node traffic. Others need the ability to imitate the behavior of thousands of individual users making diverse requests in terms of prompt size and data throughput. Testing at-scale is vital. So is test flexibility. Minor mistakes in network configurations can lead to problems that, like link flapping, do not emerge clearly until the entire system is under stress. These include seemingly simple decisions such as VLAN tagging, queue mapping, and buffer allocations that turn out to be inadequate. Each of them can silently degrade performance to the point where it becomes painfully obvious. Take an unexpected level of packet loss during peak loads. That may be because of misconfigurations in the thresholds set for techniques like priority flow control. This allows individual flow for different data streams, but poorly chosen thresholds, just like inadequate buffers in switch ports, can cause unexpected losses during bursts. If those are synchronized events, such as training weight updates, the effects can be widespread. Troubleshooting for 800G and 1.6T Data Center Fabrics Of course, troubleshooting such issues using conventional techniques is challenging. The scale and interdependencies of AI workloads complicate root cause isolation, as issues often involve multiple components and network layers simultaneously. Testing infrastructure needs to be designed so that users can easily adapt to different scenarios as they track down issues. In addition, test strategies should first detect the potential for these problems and then home in on affected queues or ports. Without specialized equipment, it would take an entire data center to exercise the target data center to the extent needed to detect these situations. A far more efficient solution is to use hardware and software built for xPU and client emulation at scale. Purpose built 800G and 1.6T testing platforms such as VIAVI TestCenter and its automation tools allow testing across varying frame sizes, data sizes, port speeds, and AI workload traffic patterns. Through advanced reporting and interactive dashboards, this combination delivers the ability to find signs of problems and assess the combinations of events that cause them to appear. The results empower network architects to fix issues and fine-tune settings. By integrating traffic emulation, performance benchmarking, and flow-level analytics into the development and test process, network and infrastructure teams who need to create AI-ready systems are better equipped to make informed decisions and reduce risk, increasing confidence in the final deployment. Learn more about VIAVI’s AI Data Center Network Testing solutions. Categories: Industry Trends Tags: AI Data Center Testing , AI Traffic , Artificial Intelligence

(NASDAQ: NOMA) (“Nomadar” or the “Company”), a global platform operating at the intersection of sports, tourism, technology, and infrastructure, today announced that the Cádiz Music Stadium concert series has received national recognition at the Music & Sport Summit in Madrid, highlighting the platform as a leading example in Spain of the transformation of football stadiums into large-scale live entertainment venues. By converting underutilized stadium capacity into multi-event entertainment platforms, Nomadar is establishing a repeatable operating model that supports recurring revenue opportunities, increased asset efficiency, and long-term value creation across its venue portfolio. Nomadar is not simply hosting eventsit is building a scalable infrastructure layer for live entertainment across Europe. title: Overcoming Marketplace Complexity for Ecommerce Success
summary: Discover how marketplace complexity hinders ecommerce growth and learn strategies to align your brand across multiple channels.
body_text: When ecommerce growth slows, it’s rarely one issue. It’s a series of small disconnects across your business. As brands expand across the global marketplace, those gaps become harder to spot and fix. That’s what marketplace complexity really is. Why ecommerce feels so hard right now Brands are managing more than ever: More channels Higher customer expectations Constantly shifting marketplace rules Pricing pressure from multiple sellers Inventory and fulfillment challenges Too many tools, not enough clarity Together, these create marketplace complexity that makes it harder to maintain strong ecommerce performance. 4 questions to diagnose what’s holding you back Instead of guessing where the issue is, break it down. #1 Are enough shoppers finding your products? If traffic is flat, don’t assume demand is the issue. Are your best products ranking where they should? Are your titles, keywords, and attributes optimized? Are your ad dollars supporting your priority SKUs? Are you showing up consistently across the global marketplace? #2 Are product pages doing enough to convert? A lot of brands lose sales right on the PDP. Are your images answering shopper questions quickly? Does your copy clearly explain value and differentiation? Are reviews helping or hurting conversion? Is your content consistent across every major channel? #3 Are pricing issues quietly hurting performance? You can drive traffic and still lose if pricing is working against you. Are you losing margin through discounting? Are unauthorized sellers affecting price perception? Are inconsistent prices across channels creating friction? Are you losing the Buy Box too often? Pricing impacts both competitiveness and brand perception across the global marketplace. #4 Are stock and fulfillment problems costing you sales? A surprising number of growth issues are operational. Which SKUs go out of stock most often? Where are ship times hurting conversion? Are returns pointing to content issues or fulfillment issues? Are you set up to stay available during demand spikes? What this can look like in practice When these areas are aligned, the impact becomes clear. Zyliss , for example, increased conversion by 22% on its #1 SKU after improving product page clarity. Small, focused changes can drive stronger ecommerce performance. Bringing it all together Managing marketplace complexity requires a connected approach. Instead of optimizing in silos, brands need alignment across: Content Pricing Operations When these work together, teams can reduce reactive work, maintain consistency, and make faster decisions across the global marketplace. Marketplace complexity isn’t going away As brands expand across the global marketplace, the number of variables will only continue to grow. The difference is how well those variables are managed. Pattern helps brands connect every part of their business. From content to pricing to operations, everything works together instead of in isolation. The result is less guesswork, better alignment, and stronger ecommerce performance over time. FAQs What is marketplace optimization? Marketplace optimization is the process of improving how your products perform across ecommerce platforms by aligning content, pricing, and operations. It focuses on increasing visibility, conversion, and consistency to drive stronger ecommerce performance across every channel. What are the 4 types of marketplace complexity? Marketplace complexity typically shows up in four key areas: Discovery Conversion Pricing Operations These areas are interconnected, and issues in one often affect the others. How does marketplace complexity impact business strategies? Marketplace complexity makes it harder to execute a consistent strategy across the global marketplace. As brands expand, teams often become reactive, which slows decision-making and limits growth. What factors contribute to marketplace optimization? Marketplace optimization is driven by three core factors: Content Pricing Operations Strong ecommerce performance depends on how well these elements work together. How does a marketplace work? An ecommerce marketplace connects buyers and sellers on a single platform, using algorithms to rank products based on relevance, pricing, content, and availability. Understanding how does a marketplace work is important because each platform evaluates performance differently.
